questions.question: What does associativity say about the expression $a\star b\star c$?
options: The order of $a,b,c$ may be changed freely.
It forces every element to have an inverse.
The operation must have an identity element.
Regrouping by parentheses gives the same result.

questions.question: Why is subtraction a standard example of a non-associative operation?
options: Subtraction is not a rule with two inputs.
Subtraction has no identity element.
Subtraction is commutative but not closed.
Usually $(a-b)-c$ and $a-(b-c)$ are different.

questions.question: Let $a\star b=a+b+1$ on $\mathbb{R}$. What are $(a\star b)\star c$ and $a\star(b\star c)$?
options: Both are $a+b+c$.
They are $a+2b+c+1$ and $a+b+2c+1$.
They are $a+b+c+1$ and $a+b+c+2$.
Both are $a+b+c+2$.

questions.question: Let $a\star b=a+2b$ on $\mathbb{R}$. Which computation shows non-associativity?
options: $(1\star2)\star3=17$ and $1\star(2\star3)=17$.
The rule is not closed on $\mathbb{R}$.
$(1\star2)\star3=3$ but $1\star(2\star3)=3$.
$(1\star2)\star3=11$ but $1\star(2\star3)=17$.

questions.question: If an operation is associative, does it necessarily have an identity element?
options: Yes. The identity is automatically the first element of the set.
No, because associative operations cannot be binary operations.
No. Associativity alone does not produce an identity element.
Yes, but only if the set is finite.

questions.question: Why does associativity have to hold for all triples rather than just one example?
options: One successful triple does not rule out another triple with different parenthesised values.
Associativity is a property of a single chosen triple, so one example settles it completely.
Associativity is never tested by examples.
Associativity is checked only at the identity element.

questions.question: What is the shortest kind of calculation that can disprove associativity?
options: A proof that every triple works.
A demonstration that an identity exists.
A check that $a\star b=b\star a$ for one pair.
One triple with $(a\star b)\star c\ne a\star(b\star c)$.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$, is the operation $a\star b=\max(a,b)$ associative?
options: No, because $\max(a,b)$ is never equal to $a$.
Only when all three inputs are positive.
Yes, both groupings give the maximum of $a,b,c$.
No, because maximum is not closed on $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Function composition is associative. What does this say about $f\circ g\circ h$?
options: $f\circ g=g\circ f$ for all functions.
$f\circ g\circ h$ is defined for all functions with no domain conditions.
Every function has a composition inverse.
$(f\circ g)\circ h=f\circ(g\circ h)$ whenever the compositions are defined.

questions.question: Why does associativity make products of four or more elements easier to write?
options: It implies the product is independent of the order of the factors.
It fixes the bracketing $((ab)c)d$ as the one convention to use.
It holds for triples only, so each fourfold product must be checked.
All bracketings give the same value, so the brackets can be dropped.

questions.question: On any set $A$, define $a\star b=a$ for all $a,b\in A$. Is this operation associative?
options: Yes, both $(a\star b)\star c$ and $a\star(b\star c)$ equal $a$.
No, because the second input is ignored.
Only if the operation is also commutative.
No, unless $A$ has exactly one element.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}$ let $a\star b=\frac{a+b}{2}$. This operation is commutative. Is it associative?
options: No: $(0\star0)\star4=2$ but $0\star(0\star4)=1$
Yes: since $a\star b=b\star a$, it does not matter which pair is combined first
Yes: both groupings average the same three numbers and equal $\frac{a+b+c}{3}$
Yes, but only for inputs with $a\le b\le c$
